# PART ONE: THE CLAIM

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

An elephant is dying in a lake.

He is the head of his herd, immense and unbothered, and he has waded in to drink. Then a crocodile takes him by the foot and will not let go. The elephant is the stronger animal, but the water is the crocodile’s country, and strength counts for nothing there. The struggle lasts, in the telling, 1,000 years. His herd strains to save him, the cows crying out, the great bulls gripping him from behind to pull him back, and the Bhāgavata says plainly that they could not. At the end of everything, sinking, the elephant does the only thing left to him. He tears a lotus from the water with his trunk, lifts it toward a sky he can no longer clearly see, and cries out to the one he cannot see at all.

And the one he cannot see comes.

The Bhāgavata Purāṇa tells what happens next with a precision that is itself an argument.

> **so ‘ntaḥsarasy urubalena gṛhīta ārto, dṛṣṭvā garutmati hariṃ kha
> upāttacakram** **utkṣipya sāmbujakaraṃ giram āha kṛcchrāt,
> nārāyaṇākhilaguro bhagavan namas te**
>
> Seized within the lake by a thing of enormous strength, in agony,
> seeing Hari in the sky on the back of Garuḍa, his eagle, with his
> discus raised, he lifted his trunk with a lotus still in it and spoke
> this word in his pain: Nārāyaṇa, teacher of all, Bhagavān, homage to
> you. (Bhāgavata 8.3.32)
>
> **taṃ vīkṣya pīḍitam ajaḥ sahasāvatīrya, sagrāham āśu sarasaḥ
> kṛpayojjahāra** **grāhād vipāṭitamukhād ariṇā gajendraṃ, saṃpaśyatāṃ
> harir amūmucad ucchriyāṇām**
>
> Seeing him so afflicted, the birthless one alighted all at once and
> out of compassion swiftly pulled him from the lake, crocodile and all;
> and while the gods stood watching, Hari tore open the beast’s jaws
> with his discus and set Gajendra free. (Bhāgavata 8.3.33)
>
> *Note: the motive word in the verse is kṛpayā, out of compassion. It
> is the only reason the Bhāgavata gives him.*

The word for the whole act is compassion, and the Lord in the story has no other reason for acting. The elephant has no lineage, no ritual, no merit to plead. He is an animal drowning. The one thing that reaches him is the cry.

This is the story of Gajendra, and it sits near the heart of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the book that calls itself the ripened fruit of the tree of the Vedas, because it contains, in miniature, the claim this essay exists to test. The claim is simple to state and enormous in what it asserts. The Vaiṣṇava tradition, the tradition of those who worship Viṣṇu as the highest, does not merely say that Viṣṇu is kind among his other qualities, the way a king might be generous between wars. It says that compassion is the innermost thing about him, the attribute beneath all the attributes, the reason he does anything at all. And it goes further. The Gītā and the Purāṇas argue, scene by scene and word by word, that no other conception of the highest makes mercy so central, so unconditional, so tender, and so willing to come down: not the old gods of the Veda, whose kindness moves inside the exchange of the sacrifice; not the serene compassion of the Buddha’s way, which shines on all alike but belongs to no one. The strongest form of the claim deserves to be stated plainly, because everything that follows is a test of it. Viṣṇu is the most compassionate Lord human beings have ever worshipped.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8QJN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbe75a744-737a-4d7e-9ae4-c668718be5dd_428x627.jpeg)

Brooklyn Museum - Vishnu Saving the Elephant (Gajendra Moksha)

That is a theological claim, not a neutral fact, and the traditions it measures itself against have their own replies, which this essay will honour in their place. The way to find out is to open the three books and count. That is what I did.

## A lexicon of divine mercy: from dayā to vātsalya

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The three books are the Bhagavad Gītā, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. Between them they hold most of a thousand years of Sanskrit devotion.

Compassion in Sanskrit is not one word but a family of them, and to weigh the theme honestly you have to hold the whole family in view. There is dayā, mercy, the plain word for a heart that melts at another’s pain. There is kṛpā, a tenderness that stoops toward the weak. There is karuṇā, compassion felt as a movement of the heart, the same word Buddhism made famous. There is anukampā, which means, quite literally, a trembling along with another, a shudder of fellow feeling. There is kāruṇya, the quality of being full of karuṇā. Around these sit the words for grace, anugraha and prasāda, favour freely given and never earned. And around those sit the words for a love closer than mercy, vātsalya, the fondness a cow feels for its calf, saulabhya, the astonishing quality of being easy to reach, and the family of refuge, śaraṇa and āśraya, the shelter the helpless run to. Beneath all of them lies an old and severe ethical word, ānṛśaṃsya, non cruelty, which the Mahābhārata calls the highest law of all.

These are not interchangeable. They form a rising scale, from pity for the suffering, through grace that rescues, to a love that simply wants to be near. Much of this primer is the story of Viṣṇu climbing that scale in the imagination of his devotees.

## What the counting shows

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Counting a theme is a crude instrument, but it is an honest one, and it settles the first question: is the impression real, or is it only the warm haze a believer carries away? The counting was done in two ways: across standard English editions, one consistent translator per book, and then again in the Sanskrit, where the mercy words can be traced at their roots.

The English counts show the direction. In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa the language of compassion, grace, and refuge appears at a rate of about one word in every 1,000; in the Bhāgavata, at roughly twice that rate. The Sanskrit gives the real scale. Take the six core words for mercy and tenderness, kṛpā, karuṇā, dayā, anukampā, anugraha, and vātsalya, and set them against the length of each book. The Gītā, in its 700 verses, sounds them about 10 times per 1,000 verses. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa, for all its rescues, sounds them at about a third of that rate, 3 or 4 times per 1,000. The Bhāgavata sounds them more than 40 times per 1,000 verses. In absolute terms, the six words occur roughly 570 times across the Bhāgavata’s 14,000 odd verses, against about 23 in the whole Viṣṇu Purāṇa and 7 in the Gītā. The younger Purāṇa is not twice as saturated in the vocabulary of divine tenderness as the older one. It is roughly 10 times as saturated.

The single most telling number is the smallest. Anukampā, the Gītā’s word for the Lord’s compassion at its most intimate, a trembling along with another, appears exactly once in the Gītā, in the verse the whole poem turns on. In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa it appears never, not once in six books. In the Bhāgavata it appears 45 times, in the mouths of Bhīṣma and Brahmā and Prahlāda, in the hymns of the demigods and the teaching of Kapila to his mother. The Bhāgavata found the Gītā’s rarest and most inward mercy word and made it a refrain.

One number cuts the other way, and ends up sharpening the point. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa actually uses the vocabulary of prasāda, favour, more often per verse than the Bhāgavata does. But its favour is overwhelmingly the ordinary favour of a hierarchical world: sages propitiated, kings gracious, gods pleased with an offering. What the Bhāgavata multiplies is not favour. It is tenderness. Where the older book has no fixed epithet for it at all, the Bhāgavata calls the Lord bhakta vatsala, tender to his devotees, 11 times; dīna vatsala, tender to the afflicted; and, in Prahlāda’s own hymn, kṛpaṇa vatsala, tender to the wretched. The words that grow are precisely the ones that mean a mercy with a face.

But a skeptic could stop me here. Compassion, the skeptic says, is just generic Indian ethics. Every tradition praises mercy. Sages are merciful, kings are merciful, the whole moral atmosphere is merciful. None of that makes compassion special to Viṣṇu. So I filtered again, keeping only the verses where the compassion is actually his: his mercy, his grace, a plea addressed to him, a rescue performed by him. The result answers the skeptic. In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, under a fifth of the core mercy language attaches to Viṣṇu himself; most of it is the ordinary mercy of the world. In the Bhāgavata, that share rises to somewhere between a third and a half. The Bhāgavata does not merely use more compassion words. It redirects far more of them onto the Lord. Across the centuries, compassion migrates from the background ethic of a moral universe to the foreground trait of a particular person. It begins as something Viṣṇu has and ends as something Viṣṇu is.

A tradition reveals what it believes about its Lord by what it cannot stop saying about him. The rest of this essay asks why the tradition came to see mercy as the innermost thing about the Lord, and then walks the evidence, book by book, so you can watch that migration happen in the verses.

A word on method before we begin, since numbers deserve honesty. The Sanskrit counts are drawn from the complete electronic texts of the three books, searched at the root so that no form escapes, with the false catches weeded out by hand: the warrior named Kṛpa is not mercy, and gadayā, with the mace, which battle scenes use constantly, is not dayā. Words with double senses are counted honestly; prasāda, which can mean grace but also the settled clarity of a calm mind, is only counted as grace where it is grace. The English counts use one consistent translator per book. The Gītā verses are cited by chapter and verse; the Purāṇa verses by book or skandha and chapter and verse.

# PART TWO: THE THEOLOGY OF DIVINE COMPASSION

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Arjuna’s false compassion

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The Bhagavad Gītā begins, famously, with a breakdown, and the first thing it does with compassion is refuse to trust it.

Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, looks across the battlefield at the cousins and teachers he must kill, and he cannot. His bow slips from his hand. The word the Gītā uses for what has overcome him is our word: he is filled with deep compassion, kṛpayā parayāviṣṭaḥ (1.27), and sinks down in his chariot (1.47). A little later he names his own condition, saying his very nature is stricken by the taint of pity, kārpaṇya doṣopahata svabhāvaḥ (2.7), the noun built from the same root, and for the first time he asks to be taught rather than obeyed.

Here is the surprise, and it is a large one. The Gītā opens by showing us compassion and then declining to praise it. Kṛṣṇa’s answer to the weeping man is not comfort but correction. Do not yield to this unmanliness, he says, klaibyaṃ mā sma gamaḥ (2.3); it does not become you; stand up. The most compassionate teacher in the tradition looks at a man dissolving in tenderness and tells him his tenderness is a weakness.

This is not cruelty. It is a definition arrived at by negation. What Arjuna feels is real feeling, but it is feeling curved back on itself, grief for his own loss wearing the costume of concern for others, a paralysis that would let a whole unjust order stand rather than pay the price of ending it. The Gītā calls this a counterfeit, and it spends the rest of its length minting the true coin. Real compassion, it will argue, is not the sentiment that cannot act. It is the love that rescues.

## The Lord in the heart: anukampā

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Before we watch him act, it is worth asking why he acts at all, and the deepest answer these books give is that he is not, in the end, outside us.

In the tenth chapter of the Gītā, Kṛṣṇa describes what he does within a person who loves him, and it is the verse this whole subject turns on.

> **teṣām evānukampārtham aham ajñānajaṃ tamaḥ** **nāśayāmy
> ātmabhāvastho jñānadīpena bhāsvatā**
>
> Out of compassion for them alone, dwelling within their very self, I
> destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of
> knowledge. (Gītā 10.11)
>
> *Note: the word is anukampā, which means, almost literally, a
> trembling along with another. And the compassion acts from inside:
> ātmabhāvasthaḥ, standing within their own being.*

He is not a distant grantor of favours here. He is seated in the heart, and from that innermost seat he does the tenderest thing imaginable. He lights a lamp in the dark so the frightened one can see. The Gītā is explicit that this seat is real. I am seated in the hearts of all, he says, sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi sanniviṣṭaḥ (15.15). And it draws the consequence for us: the highest yogin is the one who sees the joy and pain of all beings as his own (6.32).

If the Lord dwells in every heart, then his compassion is not the pity of a stranger looking down. It is nearer than that, and more inevitable. To ask why he is compassionate becomes almost the same as asking why you flinch when your own hand is burned. He is closer to us than that. And once he is that close, the wonder is no longer that he feels for us. It is what he is willing to do about it.

## Avatāra: mercy that comes down

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Gmv_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0b1e2cfb-21d9-437b-9ddc-09ab6d1ca47d_2714x3820.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Gmv_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0b1e2cfb-21d9-437b-9ddc-09ab6d1ca47d_2714x3820.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**Vishnu on Garuda**

The first thing he does is move. His compassion does not sit still; it takes a body and comes down.

The Gītā gives the reason in two of its most quoted lines.

> **yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata** **abhyutthānam
> adharmasya tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmy aham** **paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṃ vināśāya ca
> duṣkṛtām** **dharma saṃsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge**
>
> Whenever righteousness weakens and unrighteousness rises up, O
> Bhārata, then I bring myself into being; for the protection of the
> good, the destruction of evil, and the setting right of the law, I
> come into being age after age. (Gītā 4.7 to 4.8)

The word compassion is nowhere in the verse, and it does not need to be, because the verse is compassion with its sleeves rolled up. It is the moment a quality becomes an action.

This is what the tradition means by an avatāra, a word worth slowing down on, because it is almost always mistranslated as incarnation. It does not mean that. It means a descent, from a root that describes crossing down, the way one fords a river from the far bank to this one. An avatāra is the Lord coming down to where we are drowning. And once you hold that meaning, every descent story reads as the same story in a new key. It is never a display of power for its own sake. It is a rescue.

The Viṣṇu Purāṇa gives that rescue its most elemental form in the descent of the boar. The earth herself, in this telling, has slipped from her place and sunk down into the depths of the cosmic ocean, lost under the weight of the waters. And what the Lord does about it is not to command from above. He goes in after her.

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VX9U!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd5794646-a1e4-4c1e-ad6f-f45eff71f374_1164x1500.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VX9U!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd5794646-a1e4-4c1e-ad6f-f45eff71f374_1164x1500.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Varaha Rescuing Bhu Devi.* 14th–15th century

> He, the lord, concluding that within the waters lay the earth, and
> being desirous to raise it up... took the figure of a boar... and, the
> supporter of spiritual and material being, plunged into the ocean.
> (Viṣṇu Purāṇa I.4, Wilson’s translation)

Picture the direction of that sentence. The highest being in existence turns himself into an animal and dives, down through the whole depth of the sea, to find a drowning world and carry it back into the light on the point of his tusk. When he sets her down, the Earth lifts a hymn of pure relief. It is the same shape as the elephant and the lake, only now the drowning thing is the world, and the Lord still comes down into the water after it.

Once you see the shape, you see it everywhere in the descents. When a flood is about to drown the first man, he becomes a fish and tows his boat to safety. When the gods need the ocean churned for the nectar of life, he becomes a tortoise and takes the whole grinding weight of the churn on his own back. When the worlds have been seized, he comes as a dwarf and, in three quiet steps, wins them back. When a child who loves him is about to be killed, he tears his way out of a pillar in a form that is neither man nor animal, purely to be there in time. The costumes change. The direction never does. It is always downward, and always toward the one who cannot save itself. Transcendence, here, refuses to stay transcendent. The infinite keeps making itself small and specific and reachable, a boar in the water, a dwarf at a sacrifice, a charioteer beside a broken soldier, because a compassion that stayed in heaven would not be worth the name. The descents are the proof that his mercy is not a mood he watches us from within. It is a distance he is willing to cross.

So the boar in the deep and the promise in the Gītā are one teaching. I come into being age after age, he says, and he means it as a vow. Whatever it takes, whatever form, however far down, when the world is sinking he will not remain above it. He comes.

## Śaraṇāgati: taking refuge

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

He comes down, then. But to whom, and on what terms? The stories are strangely unanimous. He comes for the helpless, and helplessness is the only ticket required.

There is a quality of the Lord that the tradition prizes above his power, and it is the strangest of all his qualities, because it is a kind of susceptibility. He can be reached. The word for it is saulabhya, the quality of being easy to attain, and its counterpart in us is the act the tradition calls śaraṇāgati, the taking of refuge. What is remarkable about refuge is that it is the one path to the Lord that asks for no strength. You do not climb to it. You fall into it, and you qualify by having nothing left.

The Gītā gathers this into the single verse it treasures above every other, the verse the commentators call the carama śloka, the final word.

> **sarva dharmān parityajya mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja** **ahaṃ tvā sarva
> pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ**
>
> Abandon all the dharmas and take refuge in me alone; I will free you
> from all sins; do not grieve. (Gītā 18.66)
>
> *Note: the dharmas abandoned here are not morals but the whole
> apparatus of duties, laws, and careful ledgers of merit. What remains
> when the ledgers are dropped is him.*

Read it slowly and notice what is missing. No condition, no examination, no list of what you must first become. Only the instruction to let go, the promise that answers it, and then, at the very end, two words spoken to a particular frightened man. Mā śucaḥ, do not grieve, is said to the same Arjuna who could not stop grieving in the first chapter. The book that opened with a man collapsing in sorrow closes with the Lord telling him the sorrow can be set down. Refuge is the bridge between the two.

The Gītā states the principle. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa shows it happening, and it chooses for its great scene of refuge not a saint but the gods themselves at the moment they stop being gods. They have been defeated. Stripped of their splendour, the whole shining hierarchy of heaven is reduced to fugitives, and they do the thing the powerful almost never do. They admit they cannot save themselves. They flee to Viṣṇu, and the hymn they raise is one long surrender.

> Oh lord of all, great soul of all, asylum of all, undecayable, have
> pity upon thy servants; oh Viṣṇu, be manifest unto us... We,
> discomfited by the Daityas, have fled to thee, oh Viṣṇu, for refuge.
> Spirit of all, have compassion upon us; defend us with thy mighty
> power. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa I.9, Wilson’s translation)
>
> *Note: the Daityas are the demons who have driven the gods from their
> heaven.*

Notice that these are gods. If anyone in the cosmos had standing to negotiate, to offer, to earn, it was they, and the Purāṇa strips it all away before it lets them approach. They come with empty hands. That is the point the scene is making. Refuge is not the last resort of the weak. It is the true condition of everyone, and the gods are simply the first to be honest about it.

And Viṣṇu answers, not with a lecture but with a rescue. He sets in motion the churning of the great ocean, and from that churning, among the treasures the sea gives up, rises Śrī, the goddess of fortune, seated on her lotus, whom the Purāṇa calls the mother of the world and the beloved of Viṣṇu. She is not a decoration on the story. In the tradition’s reading she is his compassion given a face and a name, his favour made into a person who can stand beside him. And what the Purāṇa gives her is the tenderest promise in the book, spoken in her own voice: I will never turn my face away from that mortal who praises me as Indra has praised me. The grace the gods fled toward turns out to have been a person who was already inclined to come. The door was open before they knocked.

If the gods make the principle grand, a small boy makes it unbearable. His name is Dhruva. He is a child, a prince, whose father’s second wife has humiliated him, telling him he has no right even to climb into his father’s lap. Wounded past what a child should have to bear, he resolves to leave. His mother, begging him to stay, tells him, thou art my only refuge, I have no hope but thou, and the five year old walks into the forest anyway, to find the refuge that stands behind every refuge. When he reaches the Lord in his meditation, his whole theology fits in a single sentence: I have taken refuge with that pure form of thine, oh supreme. And Viṣṇu comes to the child. Consider what he might have said, this infinite being, to a small boy who had wandered into the woods in a fit of hurt pride. He might have tested him. He might have corrected him. Instead the Purāṇa gives him words that read like a hand laid on a small head.

> Son of Uttānapāda, be prosperous. Contented with thy devotions, I, the
> giver of boons, am present. Demand what boon thou desirest... I am
> well pleased with thee. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa I.12, Wilson’s translation)

The child who had been told he was worth nothing hears, from the highest being in existence, that he is seen, and cherished, and welcome. Dhruva had no merit. He had a wound and a longing and a single true sentence, and it was enough.

Put the three together and the shape is clear. The Gītā gives the doctrine, that you may abandon everything and simply take hold of him. The gods give the scale, that even the mighty come with empty hands. The child gives the intimacy, that the emptiest hands of all are the ones he fills first. The tradition asks only one qualification for his mercy, and it is a strange one to build a religion on. You qualify by having run out of everything else.

## Anugraha: grace to the guilty

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Helplessness is one thing. Guilt is another, and harder. It is one matter to rescue the innocent who cannot save themselves, and quite another to rescue the guilty who, by any fair accounting, should not be saved at all. Here the tradition makes its boldest claim, and it makes it on purpose, because a mercy that could be earned would not really be mercy.

The Gītā states it almost as a provocation.

> **api cet sudurācāro bhajate mām ananyabhāk** **sādhur eva sa
> mantavyaḥ samyag vyavasito hi saḥ** **kṣipraṃ bhavati dharmātmā
> śaśvacchāntiṃ nigacchati** **kaunteya pratijānīhi na me bhaktaḥ
> praṇaśyati**
>
> Even the very worst of evildoers, if he worships me with an undivided
> heart, is to be counted righteous, for he has resolved rightly;
> swiftly he becomes a soul of dharma and attains lasting peace. O son
> of Kuntī, declare it: my devotee never perishes. (Gītā 9.30 to 9.31)

And he closes the door against every exclusion the social order knew.

> **māṃ hi pārtha vyapāśritya ye ‘pi syuḥ pāpayonayaḥ** **striyo vaiśyās
> tathā śūdrās te ‘pi yānti parāṃ gatim**
>
> For those who take refuge in me, O Pārtha, even those of stained
> birth, women, merchants, and servants, they too reach the highest
> goal. (Gītā 9.32)
>
> *Note: the verse speaks in the categories of its age, the very
> categories its society used to exclude, and its point is to overrule
> them. Whoever the order pushed to the margins, the refuge reaches.*

The turning of the heart comes first; the becoming good follows after, as its result. Grace, anugraha, means a favour freely given, and a favour you had to deserve would be a wage, not a gift.

The Bhāgavata pushes this as far as it can go, in the story of Ajāmila (Skandha 6). Born to learning and duty, Ajāmila abandoned all of it for a life of theft and lust, and wasted himself utterly. This is no sympathetic sinner with a hidden nobility; the Bhāgavata is blunt about how far he fell. And then he comes to die. Three terrible figures arrive with nooses, the servants of Yama, lord of the dead, and begin tearing the soul out of him, and in his terror he calls out, loudly and at length, to his youngest son, who is playing at a distance. The boy’s name is Nārāyaṇa, which is also a name of the Lord. Ajāmila is not praying. He is a frightened man shouting for his child. But the Name has been spoken. And hearing the Name of their master called aloud by the dying man, though he called it without meaning it, the messengers of Viṣṇu rush to the spot, four armed and lotus eyed, and stop the servants of Yama by force, wrenching the noose off a soul that by every entry in the ledger belonged to them.

The Bhāgavata refuses to let us soften this into a lesson about sincerity. It stresses that Ajāmila had no devotion and no proper intonation, that his mind was in no fit state, that he meant only to call his son. The whole point is that the mercy did not depend on him. It depended on the Name, and the messengers of the Lord state the doctrine over the dying man in a single verse.

> **sāṅketyaṃ pārihāsyaṃ vā stobhaṃ helanam eva vā**
> **vaikuṇṭhanāmagrahaṇam aśeṣāghaharaṃ viduḥ**
>
> Spoken to call someone, spoken in jest, spoken as a filler of song, or
> spoken even in contempt, the taking of the Name of Vaikuṇṭha destroys
> sin without remainder: so the wise know. (Bhāgavata 6.2.14)
>
> *Note: Vaikuṇṭha is the Lord’s own abode, and the Name of Vaikuṇṭha
> means his Name. The verse lists, one by one, every way a name can be
> said without meaning it, and closes every loophole in mercy’s favour.
> Aśeṣa means without remainder; nothing of the sin survives.*

The Name belongs to a Lord whose compassion runs so far ahead of desert that it can be triggered by an accident. This is why the tradition chose, as its great parable of grace, not a good man who slipped but a wreck who had thrown his life away. Anyone can imagine mercy for the basically good. The Bhāgavata wants you to imagine it for the man you had already written off, because that is how you know the mercy is real. It reaches exactly the people who could never have reached it themselves.

There is a hard freedom in this that is easy to miss under the drama. If grace could be earned, then every soul would be forever calculating whether it had done enough, and the frightened would have most reason to despair. By placing the whole weight on the Name rather than on the merit of the one who speaks it, the Bhāgavata lifts that calculation off us entirely. The worst evildoer of the Gītā and the ruined brahmin of the Bhāgavata are not exceptions the tradition is embarrassed by. They are the proof it is proudest of.

## Vātsalya: from mercy to love

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Rescue the drowning, forgive the guilty, and you have described a very great mercy. But underneath even that, these books keep uncovering something that is not mercy at all. Mercy, for all its beauty, can still be the posture of a superior stooping to an inferior. The tradition digs under that posture and finds something warmer holding it up. It finds love, and the word it reaches for is not one of the grand ones. It is vātsalya, the ordinary, aching fondness a mother feels for her child.

The Gītā says it plainly, and saves the saying for the end, just before the final secret.

> **sarvaguhyatamaṃ bhūyaḥ śṛṇu me paramaṃ vacaḥ** **iṣṭo ‘si me dṛḍham
> iti tato vakṣyāmi te hitam**
>
> Hear again my highest word, the most secret of all: you are dearly
> loved by me, and so I will speak for your good. (Gītā 18.64)
>
> **manmanā bhava madbhakto madyājī māṃ namaskuru** **mām evaiṣyasi
> satyaṃ te pratijāne priyo ‘si me**
>
> Set your mind on me, be devoted to me, worship me, bow to me, and you
> will come to me. I promise you this truly, for you are dear to me.
> (Gītā 18.65)

This is no longer the language of a sovereign granting protection. It is a confession of affection, offered as the reason behind everything else.

The Bhāgavata turns that confession into a whole world, the boyhood of Kṛṣṇa in the cow country of Vraja, where Bhagavān is loved not as a king but as a child and a darling, and where the tenderness runs downward, into smallness, because that is what love does. One day, says the Bhāgavata, Yaśodā was fondling her little son in her lap when the babe suddenly grew too heavy for her arms.

Yashoda milks a cow, while an infant Krishna hugs her, painting by Raja Ravi Varma

> **ekadāroham ārūḍhaṃ lālayantī sutaṃ satī** **garimāṇaṃ śiśor voḍhuṃ
> na sehe girikūṭavat**
>
> Once, fondling her son whom she had lifted onto her lap, the good
> mother could no longer bear the child’s weight, as if it were the peak
> of a mountain. (Bhāgavata 10.7.18)

For an instant the weight of the whole universe presses through the body of a one year old, and then it is gone, and he is only her boy again. The tradition loves to tell how she once tried to tie that boy to a mortar to keep him from mischief, and the Bhāgavata gives the mother a word of her own as she reaches for the rope: arbhaka vatsalā, tender to her child (10.9.12). The Lord whom nothing in existence can bind stood before her with his face cast down and let the rope be knotted around him. Kuntī, remembering that scene years later in her great prayer, confesses that it bewilders her past all the cosmic visions.

> **gopy ādade tvayi kṛtāgasi dāma tāvad, yā te
> daśāśrukalilāñjanasambhramākṣam** **vaktraṃ ninīya bhayabhāvanayā
> sthitasya, sā māṃ vimohayati bhīr api yad bibheti**
>
> When you had misbehaved, the cowherd woman took up the rope to bind
> you, and you stood with frightened eyes brimming with tears, the black
> of them smearing, your face cast down in fear. That state of yours
> bewilders me, that Fear itself is afraid of you. (Bhāgavata 1.8.31)

The one who holds the cosmos consents to be held. That is what he is willing to become for the sake of being loved.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ba5M!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F65712586-527e-4e63-98ff-81c4300d1acb_2233x3400.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**Krishna and the Gopis Gather for Rasamandala.** 1720–30

And when the cowherd women come to him in the night, the Bhāgavata says something that reads almost as a definition of grace as tenderness. Revealing himself in as many forms as there were women, he was with each of them, so that not one was left standing alone while another was embraced (10.33). No one is a spare. Each is danced with as though she were the only one. And then, in the middle of that overwhelming scene, the Bhāgavata pauses on a gesture so small it could be missed.

> **tāsāṃ rati vihāreṇa śrāntānāṃ vadanāni saḥ** **prāmṛjat karuṇaḥ
> premṇā śantamenāṅga pāṇinā**
>
> And he, the compassionate one, with love, wiped the faces of those
> girls, tired from the play of the dance, with the hand that soothes
> most. (Bhāgavata 10.33.21; some editions number it 10.33.20)
>
> *Note: every word is carrying weight. Karuṇaḥ, the compassionate one.
> Premṇā, with love. Śantamena pāṇinā, with the most soothing of hands.*

The vocabulary we have followed through the drowning elephant and the descending boar is spent here on drying the sweat from a dancer’s cheek. The hand that broke the crocodile’s jaws is the hand that wipes a tired face.

This is why the whole subject finally resolves into love rather than mercy. Mercy answers need, and if need were the whole story, then once we were safe he would have no more reason to attend to us. But love is not answering a need. Love wants to be near. It is the difference between a rescuer, who is done when you are pulled from the water, and a mother, who is never done. The reason he comes when we call is not only that we are drowning. It is that he is fond of us, that he made himself small enough to be held, that he would multiply himself rather than leave one of us dancing alone. Take away the compassion for a moment and there is still this underneath it, warm and unhurried and a little astonishing. He likes us. He always did.

## Brahmā’s verse: Bhāgavata 10.14.8

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Before the comparison, one verse deserves to stand alone, because in it the Bhāgavata states its doctrine of mercy as doctrine, and lets the maker of the worlds be the one to say it. Brahmā, the creator, has just tested the cowherd boy of Vraja and been overwhelmed by what he found, and the hymn he pours out in his defeat contains the verse the later tradition would treasure above almost any other.

> **tat te ‘nukampāṃ susamīkṣamāṇo, bhuñjāna evātmakṛtaṃ vipākam** **hṛd
> vāg vapurbhir vidadhan namas te, jīveta yo muktipade sa dāyabhāk**
>
> The one who lives watching intently for your compassion, bearing
> whatever ripens from his own past deeds, offering homage with heart,
> speech, and body, is the rightful heir to the seat of liberation.
> (Bhāgavata 10.14.8)
>
> *Note: dāyabhāk is an inheritance word. An heir does not earn the
> estate. He is simply the son.*

It is the whole theology of these books compressed into four lines. The heir of liberation is not the one who conquers his senses, though the tradition honours that, and not the one who perfects the rites or completes the knowledge. It is the one who watches for his compassion the way a farmer watches the sky for rain, bearing his own harvest in the meantime. And the word for the compassion he watches for is anukampā, the Gītā’s own trembling word from 10.11, which the Viṣṇu Purāṇa never uses at all and the Bhāgavata uses 45 times, here returned with interest at the very summit of the book. Watching his mercy is not preparation for the path. It is the path.

## The rivals: the Vedic gods, Śiva, the Goddess, the Buddha

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

It is worth pausing to say what this compassion is not, because comparison sharpens it, and because the claim this essay opened with, that no Lord was ever more compassionate, cannot be made honestly without looking the rivals in the face.

Begin with the gods of the Veda, the world these three books grew out of. Their dealings with men move, above all, inside an exchange. Indra’s strength answers the pressed soma; Varuṇa’s mercy is the mercy of a judge, who may loosen the noose he himself has fitted; the sacrifice is a contract, and the kindness of the gods is real but purchasable. The Gītā itself draws this contrast from inside the tradition. The knowers of the three Vedas, it says, having worshipped with soma and won heaven, enjoy the celestial pleasures of the gods until the merit is spent, and then, when it is exhausted, they fall back into the mortal world (9.20 to 9.21). What the offering purchases, runs out. Against this it sets the devotee who thinks of nothing else, and gives him the sentence that broke the old economy in two.

> **ananyāś cintayanto māṃ ye janāḥ paryupāsate** **teṣāṃ
> nityābhiyuktānāṃ yogakṣemaṃ vahāmy aham**
>
> But those who worship me thinking of nothing else, who are constantly
> joined to me, I myself carry what they lack and preserve what they
> have. (Gītā 9.22)

The Vedic god receives the offering and pays. This Lord carries. The difference between a contract and a compassion is the whole distance between the two sentences.

Śiva must be spoken of with reverence here, and the Bhāgavata itself sets the tone: vaiṣṇavānāṃ yathā śambhuḥ, among the devotees of Viṣṇu, Śambhu is the greatest (12.13.16). The Śaiva traditions carry a rich theology of grace of their own, and any Śaiva will present it with texts in hand. Within these three books, Śiva is the swiftly pleased one, so generous that he gives without weighing the asker, and the Purāṇas tell with awe of boons granted even to those who would turn them against the worlds. The difference the counting points to is not one of generosity but of register. His is the glory of the mountain and the great austerity, the power at the edge of things; the mercy these books cannot stop describing in Viṣṇu is the tenderness of the lap and the rope, the parent’s register rather than the ascetic’s. Those are two different glories, and the tradition at its best honours both. The Goddess deserves the same honesty. Her mercy is real and vast: in the Śākta vision she is the Mother absolutely, the one who takes up arms the instant her children are threatened, and millions have fled to her as the most immediate refuge they know. The distinction, once more, is not the amount of the love but its direction. She is the mother who fights for the child. The Bhāgavata’s boldest image runs the other way: the Lord becomes the child, puts himself below the mother, and lets her bind him to a mortar. One vision arms the mother; this one lets a mother tie up the Lord. The claim of this essay is only about where unearned tenderness toward the helpless is the defining note, and the counting answers that it is in Viṣṇu.

Then there is the strongest rival of all. The word karuṇā, which the Gītā uses for the mark of the devotee the Lord loves (12.13), is also the great word of Buddhism, the compassion of the bodhisattva who vows to save all beings. But the two compassions have a different shape. Buddhist karuṇā flows from seeing that there is, finally, no separate self anywhere, and at its height it is serene and impersonal, the sun shining equally on all. The compassion of Viṣṇu is personal to its core. It has a face and a name. It plays favourites, bending toward the one who turns to it. It weeps, it descends, it wipes a tired face. It is not the calm of one who has seen through the self, but the ardour of one who loves particular creatures and will cross any distance to reach them. Both are called karuṇā. Only one comes leaping down from an eagle.

Further west, the comparison grows friendlier. A personal Lord who loves, grieves, and gives himself for his people is the closest analogue the world’s faiths offer, and a Christian reader of the Bhāgavata will recognize much. The distinctive Vaiṣṇava notes are two: the descent is not a single event in history but a standing vow renewed age after age, and the tenderness reaches a register the theologies of majesty rarely allow, the Lord as an infant in a mother’s lap, a boy caught stealing butter, a dancer wiping sweat from a girl’s face. Where other traditions guard the dignity of the highest, this one spends it, and counts the spending as glory.

These comparisons are the tradition’s own case, stated as fairly as possible, and each rival tradition has its replies, which deserve their own essays. The claim is not that mercy is absent elsewhere. It is that nowhere else is mercy the first fact, the unearned fact, the descending fact, the tender fact, the universal fact, and the self lowering fact all at once, and about one person. That conjunction is what the verses themselves now have to show.

## The compassion he leaves behind

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

There is a last turn in the theology, and it is the one that keeps this whole subject from being merely consoling. In every one of these books, the compassion of the Lord is contagious. It does not stay in heaven. It reproduces itself in the people it touches.

The Gītā said so when it listed compassion toward all beings, dayā bhūteṣu (16.2), among the marks of a divine nature, with harshness and wrath heading the demonic list a few verses later. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa made it a scene almost too hard to bear. The child Prahlāda, tortured by his father for loving Viṣṇu, is commanded to renounce the Lord he praises, and his answer to the tyrant deserves to be set apart.

> Viṣṇu, who is Brahma, is the creator and protector, not of me alone,
> but of all human beings, and even, father, of you: he is the supreme
> lord of all. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa I.17, Wilson’s translation)

The child extends the divine protection even to the man tormenting him, and through the chapters that follow he blesses the servants sent to kill him, because he has caught the Lord’s own compassion from the Lord who dwells in every heart and he cannot unlearn it. Behind all of this stands an old and severe conviction, older than any of these books, that non cruelty, ānṛśaṃsya, is the highest law there is, higher than caste, higher than ritual, higher than duty. When your particular duty and simple mercy come into conflict, that conviction says, choose mercy.

This is why the compassion of Viṣṇu is not sentimentality. It makes a demand. If the deepest thing about the Lord is that he trembles with the suffering of a drowning animal, then the deepest thing we can become is someone who trembles too.

With that theology in hand, we can now walk the evidence itself, and watch these five movements surface, book by book, in the verses.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# PART THREE: THE TEXTUAL SURVEY, BOOK BY BOOK

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This is the survey a primer owes you. We take each text in turn, walk its compassion verses, quote the ones that carry weight, and account for the rest by reference so nothing is hidden. The five movements of Part two are the lens: watch for the Lord who indwells, descends, shelters, forgives, and loves.

## The Bhagavad Gītā

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The Gītā is short, so we can name every one of its compassion verses. They fall into five natural groups, and together they are the seed of everything the Purāṇas will later grow.

**The pity that is corrected.** The Gītā’s first three uses of the mercy vocabulary are all negative, and deliberately so. Arjuna is overcome by compassion, kṛpayā parayāviṣṭaḥ, at the sight of his kinsmen (1.27), his eyes filling with tears, kṛpayāviṣṭam aśru pūrṇa (2.1), until he confesses that his nature is stricken by the taint of pity, kārpaṇya (2.7). Kṛṣṇa’s rebuke, do not yield to unmanliness (2.3), is the hinge of the whole poem: the feeling Arjuna calls compassion is the feeling the Gītā means to replace. These are the only verses where the mercy word names a human failing rather than a divine glory, and the contrast is the point.

**His compassion.** Against that counterfeit stands the true coin, and it is named exactly once, at the center of the poem, in the verse this entire tradition turns on. Out of compassion for them, anukampā, dwelling in their hearts, I destroy the darkness of ignorance with the lamp of knowledge (10.11). Here compassion is the Lord’s own inner act. Its precondition is stated at 15.15, I am seated in the hearts of all, and its human echo at 12.13, the devotee dear to the Lord is friendly and compassionate, maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca, and at 16.2, where compassion toward beings, dayā bhūteṣu, stands among the qualities of the divine nature, with harshness, pāruṣya, listed among the demonic marks two verses later (16.4).

**His grace.** The Gītā’s language of grace is the word prasāda and the word anugraha. Arjuna receives the supreme teaching, he says, by the Lord’s grace, mad anugrahāya (11.1). And the promise of grace runs through the closing chapter like a refrain: by my grace you will pass beyond all difficulties (18.58), by his grace you attain supreme peace and the eternal abode (18.62), and at the very end Arjuna’s own confession, by your grace, tvat prasādāt, my delusion is destroyed and my memory regained (18.73), with the earlier promise that by my grace, mat prasādāt, the devotee attains the imperishable abode (18.56). Grace here is not earned; it is received.

**His refuge.** The Gītā’s supreme verse is a verse of refuge. Abandon all dharmas and take refuge in me alone; I will free you from all sins; do not grieve (18.66), which it prepares four verses earlier.

> **tam eva śaraṇaṃ gaccha sarvabhāvena bhārata** **tatprasādāt parāṃ
> śāntiṃ sthānaṃ prāpsyasi śāśvatam**
>
> Go to him alone for refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata; by his
> grace you will attain the supreme peace and the eternal abode. (Gītā
> 18.62)

And it echoes with those who take refuge in me alone cross beyond māyā, his own bewildering power that no effort crosses (7.14). The refuge is open to all without exception, even, the poem insists, the worst evildoer (9.30 to 9.31) and those of the lowliest birth (9.32).

**His love.** Beneath refuge lies affection. The friend of all beings, suhṛt (5.29), becomes, by the last chapter, a lover: you are dearly loved by me (18.64), you are dear to me (18.65), and the whole litany of the devotee who is dear to the Lord (12.13 to 12.20). Even the terror of the cosmic vision ends in a plea to the Lord’s tenderness.

> **tasmāt praṇamya praṇidhāya kāyaṃ, prasādaye tvām aham īśam īḍyam**
> **piteva putrasya sakheva sakhyuḥ, priyaḥ priyāyārhasi deva soḍhum**
>
> Therefore, bowing down and prostrating my body, I beg your grace, O
> Lord worthy of worship: as a father bears with a son, as a friend with
> a friend, as a lover with the beloved, so should you bear with me, O
> Deva. (Gītā 11.44)
>
> *Note: Arjuna has just seen the form that swallows worlds, and the
> analogies he reaches for are the three most intimate relationships a
> human being has.*

That is the entire compassion vocabulary of the Gītā: 30 loci, 30 distinct places where the mercy vocabulary occurs, by exact count in the Sanskrit, and of them all but three, the cluster of Arjuna’s corrected pity, belong to the Lord’s own mercy, grace, refuge, or love, 9 in every 10. For so short a text to place its single use of anukampā at its exact center, and to close on I will free you from all sins, do not grieve, tells you where its heart lies.

## The Viṣṇu Purāṇa

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The Viṣṇu Purāṇa carries 111 verses where the mercy is his, and they cluster exactly where you would expect: heaviest in Book One, which tells the great devotional stories, and in Book Five, the life of Kṛṣṇa, and thinnest in the books of cosmography and genealogy between them. That distribution is itself a lesson. Compassion gathers around narrative, around a person in trouble and a Lord who answers.

**Book One** holds the richest seam, 31 loci spread across chapters 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, and 11 through 20. It opens in a key of grace, the sage receiving his knowledge through the favour of the Lord (I.1), and rises through the cosmogony to the descent of the boar, who plunges into the ocean to raise the drowning Earth (I.4), the first great picture of compassion as rescue. Its devotional heart is a run of four episodes. The gods, defeated, flee to Viṣṇu as the asylum of all, crying have pity upon thy servants, and from the churning that follows rises Śrī, his grace made into a goddess (I.9). The slighted child Dhruva calls him his only refuge and hears in return, I am well pleased with you (I.11 to I.12). The ideal king Pṛthu, a portion of Viṣṇu, is praised as compassionate and kind (I.13). And the tortured child Prahlāda declares that Viṣṇu is the creator and protector not of himself alone but of all beings, even of the father tormenting him (I.17 to I.20). When the Lord at last appears before him, the boy’s greeting compresses the whole book into an epithet.

> **deva prapannārtihara prasādaṃ kuru keśava** **avalokanadānena bhūyo
> māṃ pāvayācyuta**
>
> O Deva, remover of the pain of those who come to you, be gracious,
> Keśava; purify me again, Acyuta, by the gift of your glance. (Viṣṇu
> Purāṇa I.20.16)
>
> *Note: prapannārtihara, remover of the pain of the refuged, is the
> Purāṇa’s own compound for the whole doctrine, and it returns on other
> lips later in the book (V.23.31).*

Chapters 14 and 15 add the propitiation hymns of Dhruva’s line, where Viṣṇu is the refuge and the giver of boons.

**Book Two**, the book of cosmography and the earth’s geography, is nearly silent on mercy, with only 3 loci (chapters 2, 6, 12). The one that matters comes in the tale of the royal ascetic Bharata, where the language of taking refuge in the supreme surfaces amid an otherwise diagrammatic book, a reminder that even the map of the worlds is drawn around a Lord one can flee to.

**Book Three**, on the Vedas, the sages, and dharma, gives 6 loci (chapters 2, 7, 8). Here compassion appears less as rescue than as law.

> **dayā samastabhūteṣu titikṣā nātimānitā** **satyaṃ śaucam anāyāso
> maṅgalaṃ priyavāditā**
>
> Compassion toward all beings, forbearance, freedom from arrogance,
> truthfulness, purity, contentment, auspicious conduct, and gentle
> speech. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa III.8.36, from the duties by which Viṣṇu is
> pleased)

Dayā heads the list of the duties that please him, so that mercy toward creatures becomes a form of worship. The book’s teaching on right conduct quietly makes kindness the substance of religion.

**Book Four**, the long dynastic chronicle, carries 13 loci (chapters 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 13, 15, 18). Amid the king lists, devotion keeps breaking through: the refrain to that Viṣṇu I fly for refuge recurs, and the story of the pious king Ambarīṣa, the great devotee of Hari, shows the Lord defending the one who takes shelter in him. Even a genealogy, in this Purāṇa, cannot go many chapters without someone fleeing to the Lord.

**Book Five**, the life of Kṛṣṇa, is the second great reservoir, 52 loci across more than 20 chapters (1, 3, 6, 7, 10 through 13, 18 through 20, 25 through 30, 33 through 38). Here compassion becomes biography. Kṛṣṇa grants liberation to the demoness Pūtanā, who came to kill him and received the reward of a mother instead (V.5 in the wider tradition, echoed here); he subdues the serpent Kāliya but spares his life at the pleading of the serpent’s wives; he lifts Mount Govardhana as a literal shelter, holding the mountain over the cowherds and their cattle to save them from the storm (V.10 to V.13); and through the Vraja chapters he is the protector, the refuge, the beloved of the cowherd people. The concentration of mercy language here, second only to Book One, is the Viṣṇu Purāṇa already leaning toward the Bhāgavata’s Kṛṣṇa.

**Book Six**, on the dissolution of the world and the horrors of the Kali age, the last and darkest age of the cosmic cycle, closes the Purāṇa with 6 loci (chapters 7, 8) and one consoling doctrine: at the end of time, when every other refuge fails, the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu saves. The book that describes the darkest age makes the darkest age the easiest to be rescued from, because the Lord’s compassion meets the Kali yuga devotee with the least required of any. It is a fitting last word, mercy scaled to human weakness.

Read across all six books, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa shows compassion as something Viṣṇu reliably does, a settled attribute expressed in rescue after rescue. What it has not yet done, and what the Bhāgavata will, is make that mercy the very air the book breathes.

## The Bhāgavata Purāṇa

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Here the theme floods the book. There are 626 loci where the mercy is his, spread across all twelve skandhas, the trunks, as the Bhāgavata calls its books, and the introductory Māhātmya, with the greatest concentration by far in the tenth skandha, the life of Kṛṣṇa. If the Viṣṇu Purāṇa shows compassion as something Viṣṇu does, the Bhāgavata shows it as the weather of the whole world he moves through. We take it skandha by skandha.

**The Māhātmya**, the preamble in praise of the Bhāgavata itself, already sets the key with 17 loci (discourses 1, 2, 4, 5, 6). It tells of Devotion personified as a grieving mother restored to youth by the recitation of the Lord’s stories, and of sinners lifted to liberation simply by hearing them. Before the book proper begins, its subject is announced: the mercy of Hari, and the ease with which it can be received.

**Skandha One**, 44 loci across nearly every discourse (1 through 19), is the frame, and it is thick with compassion because it is a book of deaths and refuges. Kṛṣṇa is remembered as the friend whom, out of affection, Yudhiṣṭhira made his counsellor, envoy, and charioteer. Kuntī prays to him recalling how the mother Yaśodā once bound him with a cord while he stood with his face cast down. And the dying Bhīṣma, the grand old warrior of the Mahābhārata, on his bed of arrows, gives the skandha its great testimony.

> **tathāpy ekāntabhakteṣu paśya bhūpānukampitam** **yan me ‘sūṃs
> tyajataḥ sākṣāt kṛṣṇo darśanam āgataḥ**
>
> Yet see, O king, his compassion for those who are devoted to him
> alone: Kṛṣṇa himself has come into my sight at this hour, as I give up
> my life. (Bhāgavata 1.9.22)

The word Bhīṣma chooses is anukampitam, the trembling word, and the book opens with the Lord attending personally at a deathbed, which is the whole argument in a single image.

**Skandha Two**, 19 loci (discourses 2, 4, 5, 7 through 10, 19), is the cosmology taught by Śuka, the young sage who narrates the whole Purāṇa, and its compassion is metaphysical: the Lord assumes his forms and unfolds the worlds not from need but as an act of grace toward the beings who will inhabit them. Even creation, here, is a kindness. And before Śuka will teach a syllable of that cosmology, he bows, and his invocation names exactly whom this Lord purifies.

> **kirātahūṇāndhrapulindapulkaśā, ābhīraśumbhā yavanāḥ khasādayaḥ**
> **ye ‘nye ca pāpā yadapāśrayāśrayāḥ, śudhyanti tasmai prabhaviṣṇave
> namaḥ**
>
> Kirātas, Hūṇas, Āndhras, Pulindas, Pulkaśas, Ābhīras, Śumbhas,
> Yavanas, Khasas, and whatever other sinners there be: taking shelter
> of those who have taken shelter of him, they are purified. To that all
> powerful Viṣṇu I bow. (Bhāgavata 2.4.18)
>
> *Note: these are the frontier peoples the old order held furthest from
> the sacred, hunters and mountain tribes and foreigners, Greeks and
> Huns among them. The description of the universe begins by bowing to
> the Lord who purifies precisely them.*

**Skandha Three**, 64 loci and the densest of the early books (discourses 1 through 33, especially 13 through 33), gives two great pictures. It tells again the descent of the boar, who lifts the Earth from the waters, and it culminates in the teaching of Kapila, the sage the book counts among the Lord’s own descents, to his mother Devahūti, where the doctrine is stated outright.

> **bhṛtyānukampitadhiyeha gṛhītamūrteḥ** **sañcintayed bhagavato
> vadanāravindam**
>
> Let the devotee meditate on the lotus face of the Lord, who has taken
> form in this world with a mind moved by compassion for his servants.
> (Bhāgavata 3.28.29)

Divine embodiment is defined, in so many words, as an act of compassion.

**Skandha Four**, 59 loci (discourses 1, 6 through 25, 29 through 31), is the book of Dhruva and Pṛthu. Here the Bhāgavata tells its own fuller version of the slighted child Dhruva, whose longing draws the Lord to him and who is met not with a test but with grace, the same episode the Viṣṇu Purāṇa told, now dwelt on at length. Around it stand the tales of Dakṣa and Pṛthu, kingship measured again by mercy.

**Skandha Five**, 44 loci (discourses 1 through 20, 24, 25, 31), turns to Ṛṣabha, the renunciate avatāra, and to the strange, moving career of Bharata, a king who gave up a throne for the forest and was undone there by a single act of tenderness. A pregnant doe, startled at the river by a lion’s roar, miscarried into the current and died, and the royal sage saw the newborn fawn being swept downstream, wretched, kṛpaṇam, and took it up, says the Bhāgavata, out of compassion, anukampayā, like a kinsman (5.8.7). It is the Lord’s own vocabulary spent on a human act, the kṛpaṇa and the anukampā of the great rescues given to a fawn. Bharata raised it, loved it past all his vows, died thinking of it, was reborn as a deer for that attachment, and was then given a human birth in which he finally walked free. The skandha reads his whole arc the way it reads everything else it contains: as the patience of a Lord who follows a soul through many births and many errors and does not abandon it. Even the man undone by compassion is not, in the end, undone. And even in this book’s descriptions of the hells, the Lord’s mercy is the thread by which the fallen are eventually raised.

**Skandha Six**, 27 loci (discourses 1 through 19), is the book of Ajāmila, and so it is one of the tradition’s central testimonies to grace beyond desert. The fallen brahmin cries his son’s name Nārāyaṇa at the hour of death, and the messengers of Viṣṇu wrench Yama’s noose from him, on the strength of a Name spoken without meaning. Around this stand the hymns of Dakṣa and the doctrine, stated plainly here, that to develop love for the Lord through his Name is the paramount duty of all, because the Name reaches even those who cannot reach it themselves.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gczZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F243d12b5-1c35-419e-9c5b-f6dc1617b07a_1280x1589.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Prahlada prays to Narasimha as Narasimha disembowels and kills Hiranyakashipu.

**Skandha Seven**, 32 loci (discourses 1, 4 through 15), is the book of Prahlāda, and therefore the book where divine compassion and human compassion meet. The Lord bursts from the pillar as the man lion to save the child devotee, and the child, standing before that terrifying rescue, addresses him with an epithet that compresses the whole theology.

> **trasto ‘smy ahaṃ kṛpaṇavatsala duḥsahogra, saṃsāracakrakadanād
> grasatāṃ praṇītaḥ** **baddhaḥ svakarmabhir uśattama te ‘ṅghrimūlaṃ,
> prīto ‘pavargaśaraṇaṃ hvayase kadā nu**
>
> I am terrified, O you who are tender to the wretched, driven among
> devourers by the unbearable, grinding wheel of births, and bound by my
> own deeds. When, O most radiant one, will you be pleased, and call me
> to the base of your feet, the refuge that is liberation? (Bhāgavata
> 7.9.16)
>
> *Note: kṛpaṇa vatsala, tender to the wretched. The child saved from
> the pillar does not ask for safety. He asks for the feet.*

And he in turn refuses to hate his persecutors and pleads even for his demon father, having caught his mercy from the Lord he loves. Prahlāda’s discourse on devotion makes compassion toward all beings the very substance of loving the Lord.

**Skandha Eight**, 47 loci (discourses 4 through 24), is a book of rescues, and it holds the elephant. Gajendra, seized in the lake, lifts his lotus and cries out, and the Lord alights from his eagle out of extreme compassion and draws him from the water (8.3 to 8.4). Around this stand the churning of the ocean, the saving of Manu from the flood by the fish, and the descent of the dwarf Vāmana, who grants even the defeated demon king Bali not destruction but a lasting place, mercy extended to an enemy who kept his word. If you wanted a single skandha to teach the theme, this is the one.

**Skandha Nine**, 26 loci (discourses 1 through 24), the dynastic book, keeps the theme alive through the royal lines, above all in Ambarīṣa, the devotee king whom the Lord’s discus defends against the wrath of a great sage, so that the one who takes refuge in Viṣṇu is shielded even from a brahmin’s curse. And it is in this story, when the terrified sage reaches Vaikuṇṭha itself, that the Lord makes the most astonishing confession in the three books.

> **ahaṃ bhaktaparādhīno hy asvatantra iva dvija** **sādhubhir
> grastahṛdayo bhaktair bhaktajanapriyaḥ**
>
> I am wholly under the power of my devotees, O brāhmaṇa, as if I had no
> independence at all; my heart is seized by the saintly, for I am
> beloved of my devotees and they of me. (Bhāgavata 9.4.63)
>
> **ye dārāgāraputrāpta prāṇān vittam imaṃ param** **hitvā māṃ śaraṇaṃ
> yātāḥ kathaṃ tāṃs tyaktum utsahe**
>
> They have left wife, home, children, kinsmen, wealth, and life itself,
> and come to me for refuge. How could I bear to abandon them?
> (Bhāgavata 9.4.65)
>
> **sādhavo hṛdayaṃ mahyaṃ sādhūnāṃ hṛdayaṃ tv aham**
>
> The saintly are my heart, and I am the heart of the saintly.
> (Bhāgavata 9.4.68)
>
> *Note: asvatantra, without independence. The sovereign of everything
> describes himself as the one being in existence who is not free,
> because love has already committed him.*

Nowhere does the supremacy claim of this essay stand on firmer text. Other scriptures show the highest being merciful. This one shows him owned. The genealogies, as in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, keep pausing to show the Lord protecting those who are his.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YEep!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3c283a4d-7590-485f-b344-8988c297fbf8_1380x1844.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**Krishna Lifting Mount Govardhan, from a Persian translation of the Bhagavata Purana, c. 1625**

**Skandha Ten**, 210 loci, more than a third of the whole book’s mercy language, is the life of Kṛṣṇa and the summit of the entire subject. Here compassion becomes intimacy. It is the book of vātsalya, of Yaśodā and the babe grown suddenly heavy as a mountain in her lap, of the Lord whom nothing can bind consenting to a mother’s rope. Shelter runs all through it too, most literally when Kṛṣṇa lifts Mount Govardhana over the whole of Vraja to save the people and their cattle from the storm.

> **atyāsārātivātena paśavo jātavepanāḥ** **gopā gopyaś ca śītārtā
> govindaṃ śaraṇaṃ yayuḥ**
>
> The animals trembling under the driving rain and wind, the cowherd men
> and women stricken with cold, they went to Govinda for refuge.
> (Bhāgavata 10.25.11)

He answers by holding up a mountain for seven days, and the chapter names him bhakta vatsala, tender to his devotees (10.25), one of the 11 times the Bhāgavata reaches for that epithet. Even before any of this, the skandha’s opening hymn has the gods tell the unborn child that earth and heaven themselves will become objects of his compassion.

> **diṣṭyāṅkitāṃ tvatpadakaiḥ suśobhanair, drakṣyāma gāṃ dyāṃ ca
> tavānukampitām**
>
> By good fortune we shall see this earth marked with the beauty of your
> footprints, and heaven too, made an object of your compassion.
> (Bhāgavata 10.2.38)

Grace here reaches even those who came to kill him, and the protection over the cowherds never lapses. And at the center of it all stands the night dance, where he reveals himself in as many forms as there are women so that none is left alone, and where, in the gesture the whole primer has been circling, the compassionate Lord with his own blissful hand wipes the faces of the girls made tired by dancing (10.33.21). Across its discourses, from the childhood to the Vraja years to the deeds at Mathurā and Dvārakā, the tenth skandha is one sustained demonstration that the Lord of the cosmos is also the most tender presence in a human life.

**Skandha Eleven**, 23 loci (discourses 2 through 9, 23, 26, 29 through 31), is the Lord’s final teaching before his departure, the Uddhava discourse, and its compassion turns inward and ethical. Among the marks of the true saint, it lists mercy toward all creatures, friendliness, and the absence of cruelty, so that the compassion the Lord has shown becomes the compassion the devotee is asked to become. The book that has spent ten skandhas showing divine mercy now hands it to us as a practice.

**Skandha Twelve**, 14 loci (discourses 6, 8, 10 through 13), closes the Purāṇa in the Kali age, and its last word on compassion is the gentlest and most democratic.

> **kaler doṣanidhe rājann asti hy eko mahān guṇaḥ** **kīrtanād eva
> kṛṣṇasya muktasaṅgaḥ paraṃ vrajet**
>
> The age of Kali is an ocean of faults, O king, but it holds one great
> virtue: by the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s name alone, a person is freed from
> every bond and reaches the highest. (Bhāgavata 12.3.51)

In the dark age, when every discipline is beyond most people, the sole sufficient grace is the chanting of the Lord’s name, freely available to anyone, requiring neither purity nor learning nor strength. The Bhāgavata ends where Ajāmila began, on the mercy carried in a Name, now offered to everyone alive in the hardest of times.

Read whole, the Bhāgavata does not argue that Viṣṇu is compassionate. It assumes it on every page and then shows it, from the deathbed of Bhīṣma to the lake of the elephant to the dust of Vraja, until mercy is no longer one of the things the book says about the Lord but the thing the book is.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Conclusion: The Lord who cannot look away

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Set the three books side by side and the movement is unmistakable. The Gītā defines compassion by first refusing a counterfeit, then placing the Lord’s own anukampā at its exact center. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa turns that definition into a series of rescues, compassion as a reliable divine act. And the Bhāgavata lets mercy saturate everything, until it is the innermost truth of the Lord and the whole reason he takes a body at all. Something Viṣṇu has becomes something Viṣṇu is.

This essay opened with a claim that must have sounded like devotional excess: that Viṣṇu is the most compassionate Lord human beings have ever worshipped. It is time to gather what the three books have shown and let the claim stand on its evidence. Six things, taken together, are the case.

First, mercy is his defining attribute, not one quality on a list. The counting showed it: the vocabulary of tenderness does not merely appear in these books, it multiplies across them, migrates onto his person, and hardens into his very epithets, tender to his devotees, tender to the afflicted, tender to the wretched. Other conceptions of the highest are defined first by something else, by power, by law, by austerity, by stillness. This one is defined by the trembling.

Second, his grace reaches the guilty. Boons in the wider tradition are wages; even demons earn them by austerity. His anugraha breaks the contract. Ajāmila is saved by a Name spoken without meaning it, and the worst of evildoers, the Gītā insists, is to be counted righteous the moment his heart turns. A mercy that must be earned is a payment. A mercy that outruns desert is the only kind that deserves the name.

Third, his compassion descends. Not once, as a concession, but age after age, as a standing vow. He has been a fish for a drowning man, a tortoise under a churning mountain, a boar in the depths after a drowning world, a dwarf before a demon king, a man lion for a tortured child, a cowherd boy in the dust of Vraja. A compassion that stayed in heaven would be a sentiment. His takes a body, every time, and the direction of the body is always downward.

Fourth, it is personal and tender. The great rival compassion, the karuṇā of the Buddha’s way, is serene, impersonal, the sun on all alike. His has a face and a fondness. It plays favourites with whoever turns to it. It weeps at a deathbed, lets a mother tie it to a mortar, and spends the language of world rescue on wiping the sweat from a dancer’s cheek.

Fifth, it is universal in reach. It has descended for an animal, a fallen priest, a slighted child, defeated gods, women the order slighted and the low born the order despised, and, in the end, even for the demons who came to kill him, one of whom received the reward of a mother. No one is structurally outside it. The breadth of a mercy is a measure of the mercy.

And sixth, it lowers itself. Saulabhya, the tradition calls it, the quality of being easy to reach. The one the Upaniṣads cannot find words for consents to be small, holdable, bindable, biddable, a messenger, a charioteer, a boy with his face cast down before his mother’s rope. Other conceptions guard the transcendence of the highest. This one spends its transcendence, gladly, on being reachable. Condescension, in its oldest and cleanest sense, a descending to be with, is the final proof.

Each of these, taken alone, can be found somewhere else. There is grace in the Śaiva traditions, real and richly theorized. There is compassion at the very center of the Buddhist path. There is a personal, loving, self giving Lord in the faiths of the West. The Vaiṣṇava case does not rest on any single pillar. It rests on the conjunction, mercy as the defining attribute, unearned, descending in the flesh again and again, tender rather than serene, excluding no one, and stooping all the way down, and on the claim, borne out by the counting, that no other vision of the highest holds all six at once. That is the tradition’s case, made from inside it, and the other traditions have their own replies. But it is not excess. It is an argument, and its evidence is a thousand years of text that cannot stop saying one thing.

And the last turn is the one that returns the whole subject to us. This compassion is contagious. The child Prahlāda forgives his torturers because he has caught it. The saint of the eleventh skandha is known by his mercy toward all beings. The oldest law the tradition knows, older than caste or ritual, is non cruelty, ānṛśaṃsya, the highest dharma. If the deepest thing about the Lord is that he trembles at the cry of a drowning animal, then the deepest thing we can become is someone who trembles too.

He is the Lord who comes when you call. The texts spend a thousand years saying so, in a hundred voices, through an elephant and a boar, a fugitive host of gods and a slighted child, a fallen priest and a mother with a rope and a weeping archer. And the quiet claim beneath all of it is that we were made in the image of exactly that, and are only truly ourselves when we cannot look away either.
